title: The Rackscale AI System Roadmaps That AMD Is Using To Chase Money
gist: At its Advancing AI 2026 event AMD laid out Zen 6 "Venice" Epyc 9006 CPUs (up to 256 cores, 2nm TSMC N2 compute dies, PCI-Express 6.0, 1.6 TB/sec memory bandwidth) and the MI400-series Instinct GPUs plus "Helios" rackscale systems (72 MI455X GPUs, 432 GB HBM4 each, claimed up to 30 percent more tokens per dollar than Nvidia's Vera-Rubin NVL72). The author's read: AMD has spec leadership and pricing headroom versus both Intel and Nvidia, but he is openly skeptical of AMD's 2,000X MI500 performance claim and of the low-precision math it implies, and he flags that Arm — not AMD — is the real share thief in servers.

insights.claim: In datacenter sales the roadmap, not the shipping product, is what customers actually purchase — vendors must get buyers to believe in a multi-year trajectory before any silicon changes hands.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Judge AMD and Intel on roadmap believability and cadence discipline, not just current-quarter benchmark wins; credibility loss is a multi-year revenue event.
insights.quote: Customers don’t buy products, they buy roadmaps.
insights.locator: There is a saying that has been around

insights.claim: AMD's datacenter exit around the Great Recession — triggered by Opteron server CPU bugs colliding with Intel's Nehalem Xeon recovery — cost it credibility that took roughly a decade to rebuild under Lisa Su.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Sets the base rate for how long it takes a chip vendor to recover datacenter trust — relevant when handicapping Intel's own comeback timeline.
insights.locator: Chip maker AMD lost a whole lot of credibility

insights.claim: Hyperscalers and cloud builders are actively funding an alternative to the Nvidia stack — AMD plus their own in-house XPUs and CPUs — both to keep pricing pressure on Nvidia and to hedge concentrated supply chain risk.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Customer-funded software enablement is the swing factor for AMD's AI share; watch for hyperscaler engineering commitments, not just design wins.
insights.quote: hyperscalers and cloud builders who desperately want an alternative – or two, if you count their own XPU and CPU chippery – to the Nvidia stack
insights.locator: It has taken a decade for AMD to regain its credibility

themes.theme: X86 Share Shift And The Hidden Arm Squeeze

insights.claim: AMD went from roughly 0.0 percent server CPU share in 2015 to a 46 percent revenue share of the X86 server market by early 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Anchors the pace of AMD's server CPU ascent; the remaining X86 share upside from here is arithmetically limited.
insights.locator: Su reminded everyone that AMD had about a 0.0 percent market share

insights.claim: AMD is expected to overtake Intel in unit sales of X86 server CPUs in the near term, ending a franchise Intel has dominated except for a brief Opteron window in the early 2000s.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A unit-share crossover is a headline catalyst for both stocks and a signal that Intel's server pricing power is structurally gone.
insights.locator: It will not be long before AMD is selling more server CPUs

insights.claim: Arm-based server CPUs — mostly hyperscaler homegrown parts plus Nvidia's Grace CG100 embedded in every Nvidia rackscale system — now account for roughly half of server shipments and half of server revenues, a fact AMD's own presentation omitted.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD's 46 percent X86 share is share of a shrinking-relative pie; model total server TAM in Arm-inclusive terms before extrapolating AMD growth.
insights.quote: now account for around half of server shipments and half of server revenues
insights.locator: What Su did not point out

insights.claim: The X86 slice of the server market is growing slower than the Arm slice, and Intel rather than AMD is absorbing the bulk of the Arm displacement.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Implies Intel faces a two-front loss (to AMD in X86 and to Arm in total share), compressing its server revenue faster than share-vs-AMD data alone suggests.
insights.locator: the X86 pie slice is not growing as fast as the Arm pie slice

insights.claim: Chip scarcity means Intel can still sell every server CPU it builds despite lagging AMD on performance and performance per watt for the foreseeable future.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Intel's server revenue can hold up on scarcity alone even as it loses technical leadership — do not read revenue stability as competitiveness.
insights.quote: in the current scarce market, if you can make a CPU, you can sell a CPU
insights.locator: As we have pointed out before, in the current scarce market

insights.claim: AMD's server upside may be capacity-limited rather than demand-limited, but customer CPU prejudices and installed preferences could cap how much extra volume more supply would actually convert.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Frames the question to ask on AMD earnings calls: is Epyc growth wafer-constrained or account-constrained?
insights.quote: The question I have is would AMD sell more CPUs if it made more? Perhaps, but perhaps not
insights.locator: The question I have is would AMD sell more CPUs

insights.claim: The Venice Epyc 9006 line splits processes by function: compute cores on TSMC 2 nanometer N2 with I/O dies and memory controllers on 6 nanometer, reflecting that SerDes and memory controllers shrink far worse than logic.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Leading-edge wafer demand per socket is smaller than headline node claims imply; trailing-node capacity remains a real bottleneck for AMD and peers.
insights.locator: The Epyc 9006s have compute cores etched using 2 nanometer N2

insights.claim: Top-end Venice delivers a 1.8X increase in performance per socket over like-for-like Turin parts on SPEC integer 2006, from combined frequency, IPC and core count gains.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 1.8X per-socket jump in one generation is the quantitative basis for AMD's premium pricing and for accelerated enterprise refresh cycles.
insights.locator: that yields a 1.8X increase in performance per socket

insights.claim: Venice will be the first server compute engines to ship PCI-Express 6.0 peripheral slots.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Pulls forward the PCIe 6.0 ecosystem ramp — watch NIC, SSD and retimer suppliers timed to Venice availability.
insights.locator: The Venice CPUs will be the first server compute engines

insights.claim: The top-end Venice Zen 6c part carries 256 cores and 512 threads across eight compute complex dies of 32 cores each — 33 percent more cores than the Turin Zen 5c it replaces.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Core density per socket is the metric buyers use for agentic sandbox racks; 256c sets the bar competitors must answer.
insights.locator: The top end Venice Zen 6c version will sport 256 cores

insights.claim: AMD is deliberately betting on faster DDR5 — 12.8 GHz MRDIMMs or 8 GHz RDIMMs across 16 memory controllers in the SP7 socket for 1.6 TB/sec aggregate bandwidth — rather than moving to DDR6, which would carry lower yields and higher initial cost.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Bullish for MRDIMM suppliers and bearish for a fast DDR6 server ramp; DDR6 server volume slips toward the Zen 7 Florence generation.
insights.locator: AMD is focusing on faster memory, not newer DDR6 memory

insights.claim: AMD is explicitly optimizing a CPU SKU for agentic AI sandboxes — machines executing tasks, usually in Python, rather than doing model inference — and claims best-in-class performance per rack, per watt and per dollar for that workload.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Agentic execution is emerging as a distinct CPU-heavy demand pool separate from GPU inference — a new, under-modeled server CPU TAM.
insights.quote: The idea is to give agentic AI sandboxes, which are performing tasks (usually in Python) rather than thinking, the highest performance per rack and per watt and per dollar
insights.locator: The idea is to give agentic AI sandboxes

insights.claim: AMD is segmenting Venice into at least five distinct variants — 256-core Zen 6c for agentic sandboxes, 128-core Zen 6 for cost-sensitive enterprise back office and web infrastructure, Venice HF at 5 GHz with eight 12-core chiplets and full 512-bit vectors, Venice-X with 3D vertical cache, and 2027's LPDDR5-based Verano.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Workload-specific SKU proliferation lets AMD price-discriminate across enterprise, HPC and AI host segments instead of selling one commodity part.
insights.locator: There is another Epyc 9006 chip called the Venice HF

insights.claim: The 2027 Verano variant adopts LPDDR5 instead of DDR5 DIMMs for AI host nodes — the same memory strategy Nvidia uses in Grace and plans for the Vera CV100 — converging AMD and Nvidia on low-power memory for GPU host duty.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Signals structurally rising LPDDR content in datacenters at the expense of RDIMM volume for AI host nodes.
insights.locator: a variant of Venice coming in 2027 called “Verano”

insights.claim: The author argues AMD's proliferating Venice and Florence codenames are largely marketing, since operating systems and applications see no abstraction difference between Zen and Zen c cores, only a different performance profile.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Discount codename-driven roadmap slides; the real product axis is core-count-versus-frequency binning, not distinct architectures.
insights.quote: It is debatable that any of the Venice or Florence variants merit a unique codename at all, excepting the fork between the Zen and Zen c cores.
insights.locator: We are curious to know what “Fidenza” will be

themes.theme: Pricing Power Versus Nvidia And Arm CPUs

insights.claim: On SPEC integer 2006, the 96-core Venice HF leads Nvidia's 88-core Vera CPU by 20 percent and the 256-core Venice 256c leads by 2.2X, achieved with lower clocks and half the L3 cache per core but 2.67X the cores at 3.4 GHz.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Nvidia's host CPU is not competitive on general-purpose integer throughput — a wedge AMD can use to attack Nvidia's bundled rack architecture.
insights.locator: And here, Su picks on her cousin Jensen Huang’s Vera processor

insights.claim: The performance gaps against Intel Xeon 6, Nvidia Vera and Arm's forthcoming AGI CPU give AMD room to charge a large premium and still win on price/performance even at half the average gap.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Points to server CPU ASP and gross margin expansion for AMD across the Venice cycle, not just unit share gains.
insights.quote: Those big gaps in performance tell you how much room AMD has to charge a premium for its Venice CPUs.
insights.locator: Those big gaps in performance tell you

insights.claim: Venice is expected to launch around fall 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Sets the timing window for AMD server CPU ASP mix shift and for competitive responses.
insights.locator: We shall see when Venice launches, probably in the fall

insights.claim: Nvidia offers only one way to build a Vera MGX CPU rack, at 22,528 cores per rack, while AMD supports multiple Venice 256c rack designs with differing core counts.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Configuration flexibility is AMD's differentiator for agentic sandbox buyers who optimize cores per rack rather than buying a fixed SKU.
insights.quote: There is only way to build a Vera MGX rack with Nvidia components, and that is with 22,528 cores per rack.
insights.locator: At this point, however, companies are thinking in terms of how many cores

insights.claim: AMD is holding Epyc to a two-year cadence, which the author says is about all the server industry can absorb.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Constrains how fast CPU-side refresh revenue can arrive, in contrast to the annual cadence AMD runs on Instinct GPUs.
insights.quote: The Epyc CPU roadmap is staying on a two year cadence, which frankly is about all that the server industry can handle.
insights.locator: That is all the new stuff about Venice

insights.claim: AMD is expected to try to intersect both TSMC's 1.4 nanometer A14 node and Intel's competing 14A node with the Zen 7 Florence generation, explicitly to play two foundries against each other and hedge political, technical and economic risk.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A concrete potential path for Intel Foundry to win an external marquee customer — and a lever for AMD to compress wafer pricing.
insights.locator: It is reasonable to expect that AMD will try to intersect

insights.claim: The author argues that US-based advanced foundry capacity at both TSMC and Intel raises rather than lowers the odds of a Chinese move on Taiwan, because it reduces the strategic cost of losing Taiwanese fabs.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Inverts the standard 'silicon shield' assumption — onshoring may increase, not decrease, tail risk to the semiconductor supply chain.
insights.quote: China could invade Taiwan any damned day it feels like it. . . . And with TSMC and Intel both having advanced foundry capacity in the United States, the odds are higher that it will do just that.
insights.locator: which are political as well as technical and economical

insights.claim: Florence is expected to bring Zen 7 and Zen 7c cores, shift to DDR6 main memory while retaining PCI-Express 6.0, and reuse the SP7 and SP8 sockets, with a card-mounted AI host variant like Verano.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Puts the server DDR6 inflection at the Florence generation rather than Venice — key for DRAM vendors' product timing.
insights.locator: We know for sure that there will be Zen 7 and Zen 7c core variants

insights.claim: The MI455X delivers 20 petaflops FP8 and 40 petaflops FP4 on CDNA 5, with 432 GB of HBM4 across twelve controllers and 23.3 TB/sec aggregate memory bandwidth, built from a double-chiplet Altair complex of 320 billion transistors on mixed TSMC N2 and N3.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: 432 GB of HBM4 per GPU is the headline differentiator against Nvidia; HBM4 capacity per accelerator drives memory supplier content and AMD's inference cost story.
insights.locator: The MI455X is rated at 20 petaflops at FP8

insights.claim: The MI430X targets HPC with 288 teraflops of FP64, 8.7X the 33 teraflops Nvidia's Rubin GR200 will offer on its tensor cores, while carrying the same 432 GB of HBM4 and 23.3 TB/sec of bandwidth as the MI455X.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: AMD has an order-of-magnitude native FP64 advantage — decisive for national lab and ModSim procurements over the next two years.
insights.locator: The MI430X is rated at 288 teraflops at FP64 precision

insights.claim: Nvidia is relying on Ozaki-scheme emulation of FP64 on lower-precision hardware to raise double-precision throughput, and it is unresolved whether the HPC community will accept emulated FP64 for production science.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Acceptance or rejection of emulated FP64 determines whether AMD's MI430X FP64 lead converts into actual HPC procurement wins.
insights.quote: It remains to be seen how the HPC community will feel about this.
insights.locator: Nvidia is looking at Ozaki emulation of FP64

insights.claim: The MI430X does not ship until the first half of 2027, giving Nvidia's competing part a timing lead — but only for buyers who can actually obtain Nvidia allocation.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Nvidia's allocation scarcity partially neutralizes its time-to-market advantage — AMD's practical window is wider than the ship dates suggest.
insights.quote: But only among those who can get Vera allocations from Nvidia, of course.
insights.locator: The MI430X will ship in the first half of 2027

themes.theme: Helios Rackscale Configuration And Token Economics

insights.claim: The initial Helios double-wide rack pairs 72 MI455X GPUs with 18 96-core Venice HF CPUs — a 4:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio — for 4,600 CPU cores and 18,000 GPU compute complexes per rack, shipping later in 2026.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Fixes the CPU attach rate per AI rack for AMD systems — a direct input to Epyc unit forecasts tied to Instinct volume.
insights.locator: The Helios rack will initially ship later this year

insights.claim: Helios uses UALink over Ethernet with an unnamed Ethernet switch for GPU interconnect, a Pensando Salina DPU for storage and network virtualization, and customer choice of Broadcom Thor Ultra or Pensando Vulcano 800 Gb/sec AI NICs for scale-out.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Open Ethernet/UALink plumbing plus a Broadcom NIC option is the anti-NVLink pitch; Broadcom is a direct beneficiary of Helios volume.
insights.locator: The Pensando “Salina” DPU is used to virtualize storage

insights.claim: AMD claims Helios edges out Nvidia's Vera-Rubin NVL72 on dense matrix math feeds and speeds with especially large advantages in HBM memory capacity and bandwidth.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: If memory capacity per rack is the binding constraint on frontier inference, AMD's spec lead translates into real serving-cost advantage.
insights.locator: This was for dense matrix math operations

insights.claim: AMD claims Helios delivers roughly 15, 12 and 10 percent better tokens per second per GPU at low, medium and high interactivity on Moonshot AI's Kimi K2 Thinking model, and up to 30 percent more tokens per dollar than a Vera-Rubin NVL72 rack.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: A 30 percent tokens-per-dollar edge is the quantitative pitch AMD will use to win inference capacity from cost-focused cloud buyers.
insights.locator: Su said that the Helios rack with MI455X and Venice

insights.claim: On DeepSeek V4 Flash inference the MI455X is about half as expensive per token per second per user as the MI355X even at low interactivity, and the advantage widens as interactivity rises.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: High-interactivity agentic and reasoning serving is where new-generation accelerators pay off fastest — a reason installed MI355X fleets depreciate quickly.
insights.quote: Even at low interactivity levels, the MI455X looks to be half as expensive per token per second per user.
insights.locator: Here is how AMD reckons the cost per token

insights.claim: AMD has promised the CDNA 6-based MI500 series will deliver 2,000X the performance of the MI300 from four years earlier, measured as inference tokens per second per GPU rather than per rack or at scale-out.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Note the denominator: the 2,000X headline is a per-GPU inference figure, not a system-level claim, so do not extrapolate it to datacenter throughput.
insights.quote: That 2,000X performance metric is tokens per second per GPU, not per rack, for inference workloads, so this is not scale out or even scale up performance.
insights.locator: The MI500 series will have a new architecture, CDNA 6

insights.claim: The author doubts a 2,000X per-GPU gain is achievable without 3D stacking of compute elements, and argues sub-FP4 precision such as FP2 would be needed and is dubious for complex high-resolution data like medical imaging that demands FP64.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Vendor performance claims increasingly rest on precision reduction rather than real compute gains — normalize accelerator roadmaps to a fixed precision before comparing.
insights.quote: I cannot believe we can do more than FP2 precision – FP0 anyone? – and even FP4, much less FP2, is dubious in terms of being useful for complex, high resolution data
insights.locator: I am curious to see how this is possible

insights.claim: AMD is matching an annual Instinct GPU cadence with an annual Helios rack cadence, with copper-plus-optical links arriving at Helios 500 and a possible all-optical Helios 600 in 2028.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Optical interconnect content per AI rack becomes a 2027-2028 revenue line for photonics suppliers tied to AMD's rack cadence.
insights.locator: Finally, just like the Instinct GPUs have an annual cadence

insights.claim: An all-optical AI rack in 2028 is likely premature, with the author arguing optical component production will not be ramped enough until roughly 2030.
insights.speaker: Timothy Prickett Morgan
insights.so_what: Tempers expectations for co-packaged/all-optical rack revenue before the end of the decade; supply ramp, not design, is the gate.
insights.quote: That feels like more of a 2030 move, when the industry has ramped production more for optical components.
insights.locator: The Helios 600 series could be all optical
